demandEvidence._note: Measured 2026-09-19. This CONTRADICTS the memecoin crash-protection thesis and is recorded so it is not quietly forgotten.
demandEvidence.conclusion: ~85% of newly created pools never trade. The 'token launched an hour ago goes to zero overnight' scenario is rare in new launches. Demand for stop-losses on new launches is NOT established.
demandEvidence.activeTradedUniverse: ~570 pools, 6430 swaps per 10 min, volume dispersed (top 8 = 26%)
demandEvidence.assetMix: 87.2% memecoins (BEORN, ARGUS, PI), 12.8% tokenized equity/ETF (SPYx SP500 xStock, USO United States Oil Fund)
demandEvidence.openMeasurement: Drawdowns on the ACTIVELY TRADED pools are still unmeasured. tools/snapshot.py exists to produce that number over days.

measuredDrawdowns24h._note: Measured 2026-09-19 via ARCHIVE state reads (tick at 13 points over 24h) on the 150 most-traded pools. No waiting required - the RPC serves historical eth_call.
measuredDrawdowns24h.conclusion: Stop-loss demand is REAL BUT MODEST: ~1 in 6 actively-traded tokens draws down >=20% in a day, ~1 in 20 draws down >=50%. The median pool never draws down at all. Crucially 90% of pools are UP over 24h - this is an accumulation market, so the more wanted order type is TAKE-PROFIT (sell into strength), not crash protection. OrderBook already supports both via triggerBelow; only the positioning changes.

singleBlockManipulation.threat: An attacker swaps to push a pool's price through a trigger, fills the order at the wick, and reverts the pool - all inside one transaction. The victim is dumped at a price that never really existed.
singleBlockManipulation.whyPriceBandsFail: The realised fill genuinely IS near the trigger; that is the attack, not a deviation from it. A band on execution price does not catch it.
singleBlockManipulation.whyNoTwap: Uniswap V4 removed V3's built-in oracle. There is no TWAP to read on an arbitrary pool without a hook providing one.
singleBlockManipulation.mitigation: Two-phase arm/execute with a dwell window. armOrder records that the trigger held at block N; execute requires block >= N + minDwellBlocks and re-checks the trigger. Both observations must land in DIFFERENT blocks, so a spike-and-revert inside one transaction can never satisfy both.
singleBlockManipulation.cost: An attacker must now HOLD the manipulated price across blocks and wear the arbitrage for the whole window.
singleBlockManipulation.staleness: maxArmAgeBlocks prevents replaying an old observation when price later revisits the trigger.
singleBlockManipulation.residualRisk: A well-capitalised attacker can still hold a price across a short dwell on a very thin pool. The dwell window is a cost multiplier, not a proof. Sizing it against real pool depth is outstanding work before mainnet.

designNotes.orderCarriesPoolKey: Orders store the full PoolKey, not just the PoolId. The id is derivable from the key but not the reverse, and a keeper that cannot reconstruct the key cannot route the swap. Found by running the keeper against a pool older than its log lookback - the unit tests could not have caught it.
designNotes.getOrderExists: Solidity's auto-generated getter for a mapping to a struct OMITS nested structs, so orders() does not return the key. getOrder() exists for the keeper.
